title: Counter Game
directAnswer: Louise and Richard alternate, Louise first. On a turn: if N is a power of 2, halve it; otherwise subtract the largest power of 2 less than N. Whoever makes N reach 1 wins. The winner is decided purely by the parity of the number of moves. Simulating the moves is O(log N) per turn. The bit insight: subtracting the largest power of 2 below N just clears N's highest set bit, and halving a power of 2 shifts its single bit down. So the total moves = (popcount(N) − 1) + (index of N's lowest set bit). Louise wins on odd move count, Richard on even (and Richard wins immediately when N starts at 1).

remember.pattern: Move count by bit structure → winner by parity
remember.formula:
if N == 1: moves = 0
else: moves = (popcount(N) - 1) + lowestSetBitIndex(N)
return "Louise" if moves % 2 == 1 else "Richard"
# simulation form:
# while N > 1: if isPowerOf2(N): N >>= 1 else N -= highestPowerOf2BelowN; moves++
rules: **Power of two ⇔ a single set bit ⇔ `N & (N − 1) == 0`.** Halving such a number shifts that one bit down by one position.
When N is NOT a power of two, the **largest power of 2 below N equals N's highest set bit**, so subtracting it just clears that top bit.
Therefore each subtract removes one high bit (popcount drops by 1) and each later halving moves the surviving lowest bit toward bit 0.
Total moves = `(popcount(N) − 1)` subtracts to leave one bit, plus `lowestSetBitIndex(N)` halvings to bring it to bit 0.
Louise moves first, so **odd total moves → Louise wins, even → Richard**. N == 1 means 0 moves → Richard wins immediately.
whenToUse: Alternating two-player game where the winner depends on the move count's parity
Operations that map cleanly to clearing or shifting bits
You can replace a simulation with a popcount / trailing-zero formula
Any 'halve if power of two, else subtract largest power of two' reduction
antiSignals: Players have real choices that change the outcome → Sprague–Grundy / game DP, not a fixed move count
Operation set doesn't reduce to bit clears/shifts → simulate or model differently
You need the full move sequence, not just the winner → keep the simulation
N tiny and clarity matters more than speed → the simulation is plenty
remember.takeaway: The game is deterministic, so only the move count matters — and that count is fixed by N's bits: (popcount − 1) subtracts plus (lowest-set-bit index) halvings. Parity of that sum names the winner. Simulate for clarity, or compute it in O(1) bit ops once you see the structure.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize the moves are forced (no real choice), so the winner is just the parity of the move count, and whether you can map the two operations to bit clears and shifts to count moves without simulating.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Getting the parity backwards (Louise vs Richard), forgetting that N == 1 is an immediate Richard win, or overflowing on N up to 2^64 by using a signed 32-bit type.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that the game is deterministic so only move parity matters, simulate to confirm, then give the O(1) bit formula: moves = (popcount(N) − 1) + trailingZeros(N), Louise wins iff that's odd.

problemStatement:
Louise and Richard play a game starting from a counter N. They take turns, Louise first. On each turn the current player does one of two things:

- If N is a power of 2, divide it by 2.
- Otherwise, subtract the largest power of 2 that is less than N.

The player who first makes the counter reach 1 wins. If N is initially 1, Richard wins (Louise never gets to move). Return the name of the winner.
constraints: 1 ≤ N < 2⁶⁴ (can exceed 32-bit range — use a 64-bit/unsigned-safe type)
If N == 1 at the start, the winner is Richard
understanding: Neither player has a meaningful choice — the move is fully determined by whether N is a power of 2. So the entire game is decided before it starts: count how many moves it takes to reach 1, and the parity tells you who made the final move. Louise makes moves 1, 3, 5, …; Richard makes moves 2, 4, 6, …. The two operations are exactly bit operations: subtract-largest-power clears the top set bit, halve shifts the lone bit down.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do players ever have a choice that affects the outcome?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. The rule is forced by whether N is a power of 2. So the game is deterministic and the winner depends only on the move count's parity.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens if N starts at 1?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The counter is already 1, so no move is made (0 moves). Louise never moves; Richard wins by the problem's definition.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big can N get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to just under 2⁶⁴, which overflows a signed 32-bit int. Use a 64-bit type (and treat it as unsigned where needed); Python integers handle it natively.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why does subtracting the largest power of 2 below N clear the top bit?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: When N is not a power of 2, its highest set bit has value < N, and that value IS the largest power of 2 below N. Subtracting it zeroes that bit and leaves the rest untouched.

examples.explanation: 6 (110) is not a power of 2 → subtract 4 → 2 (move 1, Louise). 2 is a power of 2 → halve → 1 (move 2, Richard). 2 moves total (even) → Richard wins.
132 = 10000100. Subtract 128 → 4 (move 1). 4 → 2 (move 2). 2 → 1 (move 3). 3 moves (odd) → Louise wins. Formula: popcount(132)=2, lowest set bit at index 2 → (2−1)+2 = 3.
Counter already at 1; 0 moves → Richard wins.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Decision tree. The game is forced, so it reduces to counting moves — by simulation or by bits.

approaches.name: Simulation — Play Out Every Move
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first: it mirrors the rules exactly and confirms the parity argument with no leap of faith.
hints: The move is forced: if N is a power of 2, halve it; otherwise subtract the largest power of 2 below N.
Detect a power of 2 with N & (N − 1) == 0. The largest power of 2 ≤ N is the value of its highest set bit.
Count moves until N becomes 1. Louise made the odd-numbered moves, so odd count → Louise, even → Richard.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each move either halves N or clears its top bit, so N loses at least one bit position every move — at most O(log N) moves, each O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Replay the game move by move, counting turns.

**The loop.** While `N > 1`: if `N` is a power of 2 (`N & (N − 1) == 0`), set `N = N / 2`; otherwise subtract the largest power of 2 below `N` (the value of its highest set bit). Increment a move counter each time.

**Why this terminates fast.** Halving a power of two reduces its bit index by one. Subtracting the top bit of a non-power-of-two clears that bit. Either way the highest set bit strictly decreases over time, so we reach `N == 1` within O(log N) moves.

**Reading off the winner.** Louise moves on turns 1, 3, 5, … and Richard on 2, 4, 6, …. The player who performs the move that lands on 1 wins, so if the total move count is odd Louise made it (Louise wins), and if even Richard did. The `N == 1` start means the loop body never runs (0 moves) → Richard.

**Why we still look for the formula.** Simulation is already efficient, but recognizing that the moves are pure bit operations lets you state the answer in closed form and explain the structure — which is what the interviewer is really probing.
approaches.insight: Because every move is forced, simulation isn't a search — it's just counting. The whole problem is 'how many forced moves until 1, and is that odd or even?'.

For a non-power-of-two, the highest set bit's value is the largest power of 2 below n; subtracting clears that bit.
Louise made the odd moves, so odd total means she made the winning one.

pitfalls: Subtracting a power of 2 that's ≥ N — it must be strictly the largest power below N (the top bit, which is < N for non-powers).
Treating N == 1 as a Louise win — it's 0 moves, so Richard wins.
Using a signed 32-bit int and overflowing when N approaches 2⁶⁴.

approaches.name: Bit Formula — Popcount and Trailing Zeros (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The insight they want. Say 'moves = (popcount − 1) + trailing-zeros, then check parity'.
hints: Map each operation to bits: subtracting the largest power of 2 below N clears N's highest set bit; halving a power of 2 shifts its single bit down by one.
So subtracts run until only one set bit remains — that's popcount(N) − 1 subtracts — and the surviving bit is the lowest one.
Then halvings carry that lowest bit down to position 0 — that's lowestSetBitIndex(N) halvings. Total = (popcount − 1) + trailingZeros.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A population count and a trailing-zero count are single built-ins (or O(word size) at worst). No loop over moves — constant time.
approaches.explanation:
Count the moves directly from N's binary representation.

**Subtracts clear high bits.** While N has more than one set bit it's never a power of 2, so every move is a subtract, and each subtract clears the current highest set bit. Starting from `popcount(N)` set bits, it takes `popcount(N) − 1` subtracts to reduce to a single remaining bit. Because subtracts remove bits from the top, the bit that survives is the LOWEST set bit of the original N.

**Halvings shift the survivor down.** Once only one bit remains, N is a power of 2 at position `t = lowestSetBitIndex(N)`. Each halving lowers that bit's position by one, so it takes exactly `t` halvings to reach position 0 (value 1).

**Total and parity.** `moves = (popcount(N) − 1) + trailingZeros(N)`. Louise moves first, so she wins iff `moves` is odd; otherwise Richard. The special case `N == 1` gives `popcount = 1`, `trailingZeros = 0` → `moves = 0` (even) → Richard, matching the rule that an initial 1 is a Richard win.

**Why it matches the simulation.** It's the same sequence of moves, just counted by structure instead of replayed — O(1) versus O(log N).
approaches.insight: The two operations are 'clear the top bit' and 'shift the lone bit down'. So the move count is read straight off N's bits: how many bits to clear (popcount − 1) plus how far the last one must fall (trailing zeros). Game theory collapses to two bit counts.

edgeCases.behavior: popcount 1, trailing 1 → moves = 0 + 1 = 1 (odd) → Louise; 2 → 1 in one halving.
popcount 2, trailing 1 → (2−1)+1 = 2 (even) → Richard, matching the simulation.

pitfalls: Reversing the parity mapping (Louise on even instead of odd).
Using a 32-bit popcount/trailing-zero call on a value near 2⁶⁴ — use the 64-bit (Long) versions.
Counting the highest set bit instead of the lowest for the halving count.

commonMistakes: Getting the winner parity backwards — Louise wins on an odd move count, Richard on even.
Forgetting that an initial N == 1 is a Richard win (zero moves).
Overflowing with a signed 32-bit type when N can approach 2⁶⁴.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Parity mapped to the wrong player
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Louise moves first (turns 1, 3, 5…). If the total move count is odd, she made the last (winning) move. Swapping this reports the wrong winner.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on large N
commonMistakesDetailed.why: N can be just under 2⁶⁴. A signed 32-bit int wraps around and corrupts both the power-of-two test and the move count.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int n = readValue();           // overflows for N >= 2^31
while (n > 1) { ... }
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
long n = readValue();          // 64-bit; use unsigned-safe ops
while (n > 1) { ... }

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Subtracting a power that's not strictly below N
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The rule subtracts the largest power of 2 LESS than N. For a non-power-of-two that's its highest set bit; using N itself or a power ≥ N breaks the reduction.

patternNote: Deterministic game → parity of a bit-derived move count. When neither player has a real choice, the winner depends only on how many forced moves occur. Here the moves are bit operations, so the count is (popcount − 1) + trailing-zeros, and parity decides the winner.
